newsitem.title: GREECE: U.S. DOLLAR TO STRENGTHEN DURING TRANSITION TO EMU.
newsitem.headline: U.S. DOLLAR TO STRENGTHEN DURING TRANSITION TO EMU.

text.p: Tighter EU fiscal policies, accomodative monetary policies, a desire for more competitive mark-block exchange rates point to a stronger dollar during the transition to EMU, bankers said.

"Cyclical positions of economies and policy settings suggest that the dollar will rally against the mark-block during the transition to EMU," said Robin Marshall, head of European Economic Research at Chase Manhattan Bank, London.

The lack of historic benchmarks for valuing the euro makes it necessary to use data on mark-block exchange rates and economies as a proxy for assessing performance vis-a-vis the U.S. economy and policy settings, said Marshall.
He was speaking on the modernisation of Greece's banking system and capital markets at a conference organised by the Hellenic American Chamber of Commerce and the Hellenic Bank Association.

The U.S economy was at the peak of the current business cycle while EU economies were either at its trough such as Italy or were riding it higher such as U.K. and Sweden,but still off highs, said Marshall.

Fiscal policy was being tightened more aggressively in EU countries scrambling to be at or below the three percent of GDP fiscal Maastricht target but steep yield curves in the mark- block pointed to a more accomodative monetary policy, he said.

This combination of stricter fiscal and looser monetary policy in the EU compared to the U.S. coupled with higher EU unemployment and especially the French and German authorities seeking to remedy it also supported a stronger dollar, he said.
But Marshall pointed to the U.S. current account deficit as a major negative for the dollar.

"The U.S. current account deficit remains a major negative for the dollar," he said. "The E.U. current account surplus mainly reflects depressed domestic demand rather than competitive exchange rates."
The head of European economic research at Chase Manhattan Bank attributed the 1996 dollar rally largely to official intervention to cover the current account deficit.

Referring to the EMU, he predicted that Germany, France, the Netherlands and Luxemburg would definitely be in the EMU group, and Austria, Belgium, Ireland and Finland were very likely to make it. As for Spain, Portugal and Italy it was possible to be in.
It will be politically difficult for Denmark, Sweden and U.K. to be in the first group of EMU countries if EMU goes ahead in 1999 and "Greece may join one day", he added.

Marshall said it was unlikely that EMU would be as hard as Germany would like because few countries met the convergence criteria and the pending danger of some deterioration in sovereign credit quality.
"...The European Central Bank may be forced to run a slightly easier monetary policy than the Bundensbank," said Marshall. --Dimitris Kontogiannis, Intercontinental Hotel Newsroom
